n: Jesus’s Galilean ministry ends. He travels south toward Jerusalem by way of Perea, the region east of the Jordan — the beginning of his final journey.

f.w: when Jesus had finished these sayings

f.g: The region of Perea, east of the Jordan River, ruled by Herod Antipas.

n: Large crowds follow him there too, and he heals them.
Pharisees test him with a hot debate of the day: may a man divorce his wife for any reason at all? Rabbinic schools disagreed sharply on this.

f.g: The school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost any reason; the school of Shammai only for serious sexual misconduct.

n: Jesus goes back past Moses to the Creation: God made humanity male and female from the beginning.
Quoting Genesis, Jesus shows marriage as God’s design: a man leaves his parents, is joined to his wife, and the two become one.

f.g: cleave = cling to, be joined to.

n: Marriage is a union God himself creates, so people should not tear it apart.

f.w: What therefore God hath joined together

n: They counter: then why did Moses allow divorce with a written certificate?
Moses permitted divorce as a concession to hard hearts, not as God’s ideal. The original design was lifelong union.
Jesus sets a higher standard: divorcing and remarrying, except for sexual unfaithfulness, is a form of adultery.
The disciples, shocked by such a high standard, wonder whether it’s better not to marry at all.

f.w: it is not good to marry

n: Jesus says not everyone can accept the alternative of not marrying — only those given that ability.

f.w: save they to whom it is given

n: Some can’t marry by birth, some because others made them eunuchs, and some choose celibacy to serve God. Latter-day Saint teaching holds eternal marriage central to God’s plan.

f.g: Men who were castrated or unable to father children; here also those who stay unmarried.

f.w: for the kingdom of heaven's sake

n: Parents bring their children for Jesus to bless, but the disciples scold them, thinking Jesus is too busy.
Jesus welcomes the children. God’s kingdom belongs to the childlike.

f.w: of such is the kingdom of heaven

n: Jesus places his hands on them in blessing, then continues his journey.
A man (vv. 20, 22 call him young and rich) asks what good deed will earn him eternal life.

f.w: what good thing shall I do

n: Jesus redirects him: true goodness comes from God alone. Then he points him to the commandments.

f.w: there is none good but one, that is, God

n: The man asks which ones. Jesus lists commandments from the second tablet — about how we treat others.
He adds honoring parents and the great summary: love your neighbor as yourself.

f.w: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

n: The young man sincerely says he has kept these all his life, yet he senses something is still missing.

f.g: Mark adds that Jesus, looking at him, loved him.

n: Jesus invites him to sell everything, give to the poor, and follow him. His wealth was the one thing standing between him and full discipleship.
He leaves sad. He has great wealth and isn’t willing to give it up — a sobering picture of a good person who stops short.
Jesus tells his disciples that wealth makes entering God’s kingdom very hard.
A deliberately absurd image: the largest animal in the region squeezing through the smallest opening. Trusting in riches makes salvation humanly impossible.

f.g: A literal sewing needle; the image is meant to sound impossible.

n: The disciples are stunned. Many assumed wealth was a sign of God’s favor — so if the rich can’t be saved, who can?
Jesus answers that salvation is impossible by human effort but possible with God. It is ultimately his gift.

f.w: with God all things are possible

n: Peter points out that the apostles have left everything to follow Jesus. What will they receive?
In the coming renewal of all things, the Twelve will sit on thrones judging Israel’s twelve tribes. Latter-day revelation confirms this role.

f.g: The rebirth or renewal of the world at Christ’s coming.

f.w: judging the twelve tribes of Israel

n: Whatever disciples give up for Christ — homes, family, land — they will receive back many times over, plus eternal life.
God’s kingdom reverses worldly rankings. Those who seem first now may end up last, and the reverse. The next parable illustrates this.

f.w: many that are first shall be last
